snapshot.capital_scaled: ₹15–50 lakh for your own designs, 50+ artisans and retail or export orders
snapshot.distribution_note: Instagram and live selling work well; apparel returns are high

tailwinds: Festive and wedding buying keeps demand for ethnic wear strong through the year.
Instagram, WhatsApp catalogues and live selling let small brands sell handwork directly, with the maker's story attached.
GI tags on crafts such as Lucknow Chikankari, Banarasi and Pochampalli give buyers a reason to trust authentic pieces.
Diaspora and export buyers pay well for authentic Indian handwork.
headwinds: Machine-made imitations sell for a fraction of the price and confuse buyers.
Apparel returns for size and fit often run at 15–30% of online orders.
Hand embroidery and weaving take weeks, so you can't restock quickly.
Middlemen control much of the artisan supply and take a large share of the price.
angle_2026: Buyers have learnt to tell machine embroidery from handwork, and they are willing to pay two to three times more when a brand shows who made the piece, how long it took and where it comes from. In 2026, proof of authenticity is the main thing handloom brands sell.
cost_basis: Estimated for a brand that works with artisans in one cluster and sells online, 2026 prices.

setup_costs.covers: Fabric, embroidery or weaving and tailoring for 30–60 pieces
Model shoot, close-ups of the handwork, short videos
Garment bags, boxes, care cards, maker tags
Creators, live-selling sessions, small ad tests

rows: 15–25% on your own site after returns and marketing
unit_economics.note: Custom sizing, clear size charts and made-to-order pieces lower returns more than any other change.

investor_probes: How do you prove that the handwork is genuine?
What is your return rate, and what drives it?
How many artisans can you rely on, and how long does a batch take?
How much of your stock is sitting in sizes that don't sell?
bootstrap_takeaway: Start made-to-order. Show samples, take prepaid orders, and only then place embroidery orders with your artisans. You avoid dead stock while you learn which designs and sizes sell.
sourcing_edge: Working directly with artisan groups in the cluster, instead of through city traders, can cut your cost by a third, lets you pay artisans more, and gives you control over quality and timelines.
licences: Handloom Mark or India Handloom Brand for handloom fabric, if you use it
Registration as an authorised user of the GI tag, if you use a GI name

hard_truths.title: Returns
hard_truths.text: Size and colour differences cause most apparel returns. Every return costs two-way shipping and often damages the packaging, so a 25% return rate can wipe out your profit.

hard_truths.title: Artisan advances and delays
hard_truths.text: Artisans need advances to buy materials, and batches often run late around festivals and harvests. Build in buffer time and don't promise dates you can't control.

hard_truths.title: Festive seasonality
hard_truths.text: Wedding and festive seasons bring most of the year's sales. Order early, because handwork can't be rushed once demand arrives.

hard_truths.title: Quality across many hands
hard_truths.text: With 5 artisans, you can check every piece. With 50, quality varies and complaints rise. You'll need written standards and someone checking pieces in the cluster.

plan_goal: The aim is ₹1 lakh in sales, mostly prepaid, before you hold stock.

plan.title: Validate and source
steps: Visit the cluster and meet 3–5 artisan groups or master artisans.
Order 5–8 sample pieces and check the handwork closely.
Show the samples to 30 target buyers and note which designs they would buy.

plan.title: Pilot batch
steps: Shoot the samples and open made-to-order bookings.
Place the first embroidery order against prepaid bookings.

plan.title: Sell directly
steps: Run live-selling sessions on Instagram with an artisan joining where possible.
Sell through WhatsApp catalogues and one exhibition or pop-up.
Send every buyer a note about who made their piece.

plan.title: Review the numbers
steps: Check returns, delivery times and profit per piece.
Keep the designs that sold without discounts.
Agree the next season's volumes with your artisans.
